name: Devbox
description: Reproducible, per-project development environments powered by Nix packages without requiring users to write Nix expressions.

large Nix store downloads
init-hook or project-script execution
prompt:
Set up Devbox from Jetify's verified installation documentation (https://www.jetify.com/docs/devbox/installing-devbox/). Start by detecting the operating system, architecture, interactive shell, available disk space, an existing `devbox` executable, and whether Nix is installed in single-user or multi-user mode. On Windows, continue only inside an already-working WSL2 distribution; do not present Devbox as a native Windows installation. Report the selected Devbox release and installer checksum or pinned Nix reference before making changes.

Preserve every existing Nix profile, channel, flake registry, daemon and trust setting, store path, Devbox global profile, project `devbox.json`, `devbox.lock`, `.devbox` directory, shell startup file, environment variable, init hook, script, and cached package. Before changing a project, show its Git status and make a restorable copy of setup-owned configuration. Apply only the requested project packages, pinned package versions, shell init hook, or global shell integration; explain that project packages are isolated while global integration changes the host shell's PATH. No credential references are needed for this setup.

Download Jetify's installer to a temporary file and inspect it instead of piping network content directly into a shell. Ask separately before installing Nix, enabling or reconfiguring the Nix daemon, using administrator privileges, creating WSL2, editing a shell startup file, adding global packages, downloading a large closure, or overwriting project configuration. Never run an unfamiliar project's init hook or script during installation. Do not update a lock file, change flake trust, enable experimental Nix features, pass `--allow-insecure`, garbage-collect the Nix store, delete profiles, or remove `.devbox` data without explicit approval. If prerequisites are unsupported, stop and link to the closest official installation path.

Verify `devbox version`, `nix --version`, the resolved executable path, platform mode, Nix daemon state, and the list of profiles before and after setup. For an existing project, inspect configuration without evaluating hooks. Otherwise initialize a disposable empty directory, inspect the generated JSON and lock file, enter an empty Devbox shell, and exit without adding packages. Prove that no pre-existing project lock, global profile, shell file, daemon setting, or store path was removed. Finish with changed paths, downloaded store size, verification evidence, manual steps, and rollback commands that remove only setup-created files and restore backups.

setup.install: Install Devbox as a non-root user from Jetify's documented installer or a pinned Nix profile, treat Nix as a separate dependency, and on Windows operate only inside an already-configured WSL2 distribution rather than pretending a native Windows binary is available.
setup.preserve: all existing Nix profiles, channels, flakes, daemon configuration, trust settings, store paths, Devbox global state, project devbox.json and devbox.lock files, .devbox directories, shell startup files, environment variables, init hooks, scripts, and cached packages
setup.safety: Do not pipe the installer into a shell before downloading and reviewing it; install Nix, enable its daemon, create WSL2, edit shell startup files, add global packages, run project init hooks or scripts, garbage-collect the Nix store, update locks, or allow insecure packages without separate approval.
setup.verify: Confirm the Devbox and Nix versions, executable source, platform mode, and unchanged profiles; validate an existing project with read-only configuration inspection, or initialize a disposable empty directory and enter a shell without adding packages, then prove no project lock, global profile, shell file, daemon setting, or Nix store path was removed.

name: act
description: Local GitHub Actions runner that discovers repository workflows and executes selected jobs inside containers for fast CI feedback.
permissionCheckpoints: container engine access
workflow or action code execution
runner image downloads
repository file mounts
network access from jobs
secret injection
artifact directory writes
prompt:
Set up act from its official nektos/act release and installation guide (https://nektosact.com/installation/index.html). Detect the operating system, architecture, shell, package managers, existing `act` binary, Git repository root, active Docker context, and whether a compatible Docker API endpoint is reachable. Prefer a signed or checksummed release through the documented Homebrew, Winget, Scoop, Chocolatey, Arch, Nix, or GitHub CLI method. Do not build an unpinned development revision.

Before executing anything, enumerate workflow files and use `act --list` for the requested event or workflow. Explain that act mounts repository content, downloads runner images and actions, and runs workflow commands with access to a container engine; it is not a perfect replica of GitHub-hosted runners. Preserve `.github/workflows`, local actions, `.actrc` files at XDG, home, and repository scope, event payloads, variable files, secret files, Docker contexts, images, containers, volumes, caches, and artifact directories. Apply only the requested runner image, container architecture, artifact path, or container reuse behavior.

Treat every workflow and referenced action as executable, potentially untrusted code. Stop before running jobs, pulling large runner images, mounting the Docker socket, using host networking, running privileged containers, writing artifacts, contacting external services, or reusing a container. Never put token values on the command line or in shell history. If a GitHub token is required, use only the opaque `secret://github/token` reference through act's secure prompt or a permission-restricted temporary secret file, and remove only that setup-created file afterward. Do not infer production secrets from GitHub CLI, environment variables, or repository files.

Verify the installed version and executable provenance, parse help output, list workflows and jobs without execution, and show the exact event, workflow, job, runner image, mounts, network mode, and secret names that a later approved run would use. Confirm that no job ran, no image was pulled, no container or volume was created, and no workflow, `.actrc`, credential, Docker context, or artifact changed. End with a rollback that removes only the installed act binary or setup-owned configuration while preserving repositories and container data.

setup.install: Install a checksummed act release through a documented package-manager channel, then detect the active Docker-compatible API without starting or reconfiguring a container engine.
setup.preserve: all workflows, local actions, layered .actrc files, event and variable files, secret files, Docker contexts, images, containers, volumes, caches, and artifact directories
setup.safety: Never execute an unreviewed workflow, pull a large runner image, expose the Docker socket, use privileged or host networking, inject secrets, contact external services, or write artifacts without approval.
setup.verify: Verify binary provenance and version, then use list mode to enumerate workflows and jobs without running commands, downloading images, creating containers, mounting files, or changing repository state.

Treat stop, reset, and delete as different operations; deletion must never be part of an automatic rollback.

Verify the Colima version and package provenance, then use `colima list`, `colima status`, and configuration inspection to report profile name, architecture, VM type, runtime, CPUs, memory, disk, Kubernetes state, mounts, and addresses. If creation was approved, start only a new named disposable profile and confirm client context selection without pulling an image or creating a workload. Prove pre-existing profiles, contexts, containers, volumes, cluster data, and files are unchanged. Roll back by stopping and removing only the setup-created profile after explicit approval and restoring the prior Docker and kubeconfig contexts.

setup.install: Install a stable Colima package after verifying virtualization and available resources, but do not create or start a Lima VM until its runtime, profile, mounts, and resource allocation are approved.
setup.preserve: all Colima profiles, Lima instances, VM disks, snapshots, images, containers, volumes, Kubernetes workloads, client contexts, SSH keys, mounts, forwarded ports, model caches, and configuration files
setup.safety: Never resize or delete a profile, switch its runtime, mount host paths, expose ports, enable Kubernetes or GPU support, install companion CLIs, pull images, or change Docker and kubeconfig contexts without approval.
setup.verify: Verify package provenance and version, then inspect profile status and configuration without starting workloads; if approved, test only a new named profile and confirm all prior runtimes, data, and contexts remain unchanged.

name: K9s

permissionCheckpoints: Kubernetes context connection
namespace selection
cluster resource mutation
log and secret viewing
port forwarding
pod or node shell creation
plugin command execution
clipboard and screen-dump output
prompt:
Set up K9s from the official derailed/k9s release and installation documentation (https://k9scli.io/topics/install/). Detect the operating system, architecture, shell, terminal capabilities, package managers, existing `k9s` and `kubectl` binaries, K9s configuration paths, and kubeconfig file locations without reading credential values. Prefer a checksummed release or the documented Homebrew, distribution, Winget, Scoop, or Chocolatey package. Avoid development `go install`, devmode Snap, Webi scripts, and third-party Docker Desktop extensions unless explicitly selected with their provenance risk understood.

Preserve every kubeconfig file and current context, cluster and namespace selection, RBAC identity, K9s config, per-cluster settings, aliases, hotkeys, views, skins, plugins, logs, screen dumps, benchmarks, and port-forward state. Back up only files that an approved change will touch. Apply the requested read-only mode, default namespace, refresh rate, or skin without replacing unrelated YAML. Keep the port-forward address on loopback and node-shell feature gate disabled unless separately approved. Treat plugins as arbitrary host commands whose environment can contain cluster, context, namespace, resource, and kubeconfig details.

Do not connect to any cluster until its server endpoint, current context, namespace, and authenticated identity are shown and approved. Never reveal kubeconfig tokens or certificates; view, decode, edit, delete, scale, restart, exec into, attach to, or port-forward a resource; create a shell pod; copy data through OSC52; run Popeye or image scans; execute a plugin; or change context automatically. Read-only mode reduces accidental mutation but does not prevent sensitive resource, log, or Secret visibility, so request permission before loading cluster data. Do not grant or broaden RBAC permissions for K9s.

Verify package provenance, `k9s version`, executable path, and `k9s info` configuration locations while offline. Validate YAML syntax and plugin command definitions without executing them. If cluster access is approved, launch with an explicit context and namespace plus `--readonly`, observe only non-sensitive resource metadata, then exit without changing current kubeconfig context. Confirm audit evidence shows no API mutation, port forward, shell pod, plugin process, screen dump, clipboard transfer, or configuration write. Roll back only setup-owned config and the installed binary, restore backups, and preserve all kubeconfigs, contexts, RBAC bindings, and cluster resources.

setup.install: Install a checksummed K9s release from an official package channel, inspect kubeconfig locations and local configuration offline, and never connect to an implicit current context during setup.
setup.preserve: all kubeconfigs, current contexts, namespaces, RBAC identities, K9s configuration, aliases, hotkeys, views, skins, plugins, logs, screen dumps, benchmarks, and existing port forwards
setup.safety: Never mutate or expose cluster resources, view secrets or sensitive logs, execute plugins, create pod or node shells, start port forwards, copy through OSC52, or broaden RBAC without separate approval.
setup.verify: Verify binary provenance, version, configuration paths, and YAML offline; if access is approved, use an explicit context and namespace in read-only mode and prove no API mutation or local state change occurred.

name: HTTP Toolkit

permissionCheckpoints: traffic interception scope
firewall and listen interface changes
system proxy configuration
certificate authority trust
browser profile launch
container or device redirection
ADB, VPN, or root access
captured data storage and export
prompt:
Set up HTTP Toolkit from its official installation guide and desktop repository (https://httptoolkit.com/docs/getting-started/installing/). Detect Windows, macOS, or Linux, architecture, package managers, existing installations, firewall state, proxy settings, browser profiles, container engines, Android tooling, and prior HTTP Toolkit data. Install and launch HTTP Toolkit without starting interception. Preserve all proxy settings, trusted certificate stores, generated CA material, rules, breakpoints, captured exchanges, exports, browser profiles, device VPNs, ADB state, container configuration, firewall rules, and upstream proxy credentials. Apply only the requested target, listen interface, upstream proxy, or certificate-validation whitelist. Keep listeners bound to loopback unless a specific device connection is approved, and never store proxy passwords directly in configuration or logs.

Traffic capture can expose cookies, authorization headers, tokens, personal data, request bodies, and private endpoints. Require explicit authorization for the exact application, account, hostnames, device, network, and time window before interception. Stop separately before changing a system proxy, trusting HTTP Toolkit's CA, opening firewall access, launching an instrumented browser, redirecting Docker traffic, installing an Android VPN or user CA, using ADB, injecting a system certificate, requesting root, rewriting traffic, exporting sessions, or disabling TLS validation. Never bypass certificate pinning, modify a third-party application, or capture traffic belonging to other users.

Verify application version, signature, executable and data paths, listening sockets, firewall state, proxy state, certificate stores, and generated CA fingerprint without exposing its private key. For a safe smoke test, use only HTTP Toolkit's documented test endpoint or a disposable local server after approval; confirm no unrelated traffic appears and stop interception immediately. Prove system proxy and trust settings match their baseline, no device VPN or ADB modification remains, and no capture was exported. Roll back by stopping listeners, restoring proxy and firewall settings, removing only setup-installed certificates from each approved target, and preserving pre-existing rules and captures.

setup.install: Install the signed HTTP Toolkit package for the detected platform, verify publisher and firewall impact, and launch without enabling a proxy, listener, certificate trust, device redirection, or interception target.
setup.preserve: all host and device proxy settings, certificate stores and CA material, rules, breakpoints, captures, exports, browser profiles, VPNs, ADB state, containers, firewall rules, and upstream proxy credentials
setup.safety: Never intercept unauthorized traffic, expose a listener, trust a CA, alter system proxy or firewall state, redirect a device or container, use ADB or root, bypass pinning, rewrite requests, or export sensitive captures without separate approval.
setup.verify: Verify signature, version, paths, sockets, firewall, proxy and trust baselines, then use only an approved disposable endpoint and prove no unrelated traffic, persistent certificate, VPN, ADB change, or exported capture remains.

name: Distrobox

prompt:
Set up Distrobox from its official project and installation guidance (https://distrobox.it/#installation). Confirm the host is Linux, then detect architecture, distribution, desktop and display protocol, package managers, rootless Podman or Docker availability, configured registries, existing distroboxes, images, containers, volumes, exported applications and binaries, desktop entries, custom homes, and `.distroboxrc`. Preserve every container, image, volume, home, package, hook, exported wrapper, desktop entry, host configuration, registry credential, and active process. Prefer rootless mode; root inside a rootless box still has the host user's file privileges, while root in a rootful box can be real host root. setup.install: Install only packaged Distrobox scripts on Linux after detecting a pre-existing rootless container manager, and never install or reconfigure the engine, socket, daemon, registries, or ID mappings implicitly.
setup.preserve: all containers, images, volumes, homes, packages, hooks, exported wrappers, desktop entries, host files, engine configuration, registry credentials, processes, sockets, and subordinate ID mappings

name: Deskflow

setup.install: Install a stable official Deskflow package after checking platform prerequisites and artifact provenance, but do not choose a role, start services, open listeners, discover peers, clear quarantine, or request input permissions.
setup.preserve: all layouts, peer names, hotkeys, switch rules, TLS keys and certificates, fingerprints, clipboard limits, addresses, logs, daemon and startup state, protocol settings, firewall rules, portal grants, and accessibility permissions
setup.safety: Never enable remote input, clipboard sharing, background service, startup, firewall access, peer trust, certificate regeneration, portal or accessibility grants, compatibility downgrade, or TLS bypass without separate scope and approval.
